newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul offers N.Korea new Red Cross talks on aid.
newsitem.headline: Seoul offers N.Korea new Red Cross talks on aid.

text.p: The South Korean Red Cross on Saturday offered new talks with its North Korean counterpart on food aid to the hunger-stricken nation.

Kang Young-hoon, president of the South Korean Red Cross, proposed a meeting on July 22 in the Panmunjom border village or at "any convenient place" on the Korean peninsula, a Red Cross statement said.
He delivered the message via a "hot line" linking the two organisations. Pyongyang has previously rejected talks on the Korean peninsula, insisting instead on Beijing.
Red Cross societies of the two Koreas signed an agreement in the Chinese capital in May to ship 50,000 tonnes of food aid, mostly corn, to the North by the end of July.
That followed a round of talks in Beijing, the first between the two sides for almost five years.
Trains carrying the first shipments of food aid entered the North on June 12.
Kang was quoted as saying the last batch of aid and an additional 2,000 tonnes of fertiliser would be delivered to the port of Nampo between July 21 and 28.
Included in the last food shipments will be 1,000 tonnes of flour and 50,000 boxes of instant noodles.
The Red Cross is the only legal channel for private aid from South Korea to the North.
Seoul's aim is to turn Red Cross talks into border contacts between the two states, locked in a bitter armed confrontation since the truce which ended the 1950-53 Korean War.
International aid agencies are stepping up food appeals for the North, warning of imminent starvation particularly among young children who are most at risk.
Floods that devasted much of the country's farmland and industrial bases in 1995 and 1996 exacerbated Pyongyang's already severe food shortages.
THe World Food Programme (WFP) launched an appeal this week for $46 million in food aid for the North. This was on top of an earlier request for $96 million.
The latest WFP appeal was aimed at helping 2.6 million children aged under six. To encourage donations, it released television footage of pitifully thin children on the edge of death.
